# Low forced vital capacity is associated with poor prognosis in physiologically stable non-IPF interstitial lung disease

**Authors:** Ryosuke Imai; Rene S. Bermea; Sophia H. Zhao; Anjali Singh; Andrew J. Synn; Bess M. Flashner; Julia K. Munchel; Mary B. Rice; Barry S. Shea; Robert W. Hallowell

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2Department of Pulmonary Medicine, Thoracic Center, St. Luke's International Hospital, St Luke's International University, Tokyo, Japan | 3Division of Pulmonary, Critical Care, and Sleep Medicine, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Current guidelines define progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) as the presence of at least two of the following three changes within 12 months: worsening symptoms, lung function decline, or new/extending radiographic abnormalities [1, 2]. However, limiting assessment to subsequent progression may miss high-risk patients: those presenting with severely impaired lung function may meet none of the criteria if later tests remain unchanged, delaying therapy initiation and close monitoring. Therefore, we examined whether baseline forced vital capacity (FVC) was associated with an increased risk of lung transplantation or death in non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (non-IPF) interstitial lung disease (ILD) patients whose FVC declined by <5 percentage points predicted during the first year after diagnosis.

## Abstract

Patients who present with reduced FVC, yet show no further FVC decline, still face poor outcomes. This demonstrates how progression-based criteria can misclassify these “stable” cases and highlights the importance of flagging them early. https://bit.ly/4oAnTgw

To the Editor:

Current guidelines define progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) as the presence of at least two of the following three changes within 12 months: worsening symptoms, lung function decline, or new/extending radiographic abnormalities [1, 2]. However, limiting assessment to subsequent progression may miss high-risk patients: those presenting with severely impaired lung function may meet none of the criteria if later tests remain unchanged, delaying therapy initiation and close monitoring. Therefore, we examined whether baseline forced vital capacity (FVC) was associated with an increased risk of lung transplantation or death in non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (non-IPF) interstitial lung disease (ILD) patients whose FVC declined by <5 percentage points predicted during the first year after diagnosis. We hypothesised that a reduced FVC measurement, even in the absence of further decline, signals advanced disease and portends poorer outcomes.

This retrospective cohort study used ILD registries from Massachusetts General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (Boston, MA, USA) from January 2015 to May 2024. Patients were eligible if they: 1) were diagnosed with ILD in the ILD clinics; 2) had pulmonary function tests (PFTs) available at the time of diagnosis and at a follow-up 9–15 months later; 3) experienced an absolute decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) % predicted of less than 5% during this interval; and 4) survived without lung transplantation through this stable period. Patients with IPF or ILD secondary to drug toxicity, radiation, or infection were excluded.

The study baseline was defined as the point 1 year after diagnostic visit. Baseline FVC % predicted was categorised into three groups: ≥80%, 50–80% and <50%, based on standard thresholds used in prior IPF studies [3, 4]. The primary end-point was transplant-free survival from study baseline to death or transplantation (censoring 20 November 2024). Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratio (HR), adjusting for age, sex, smoking, ILD subtype (connective tissue disease (CTD)-associated ILD versus interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features (IPAF; defined per the European Respiratory Society/American Thoracic Society research statement [5]) versus hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) versus other idiopathic ILD), baseline diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO) % predicted, usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, and use of immunosuppressive/antifibrotic therapy. Missing data for covariates were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations. All predicted pulmonary function values were calculated using the Global Lung Function Initiative 2012 reference equations [6].

Among 500 eligible patients (median age 69 years, 48% male) baseline FVC % predicted was ≥80% in 281, 50–80% in 185, and <50% in 34 (figure 1a). ILD subtypes included IPAF (43%), CTD-ILD (21%), HP (6%) and other idiopathic ILD (30%). Median (interquartile range) follow-up from study baseline was 27 (14–48) months. In a multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression model, patients with baseline FVC % predicted of 50–80% had a higher risk of lung transplant or death compared to those with baseline FVC % predicted ≥80% (reference group) (adjusted HR 2.37, 95% CI 1.33–4.22; p=0.005). The risk was even greater in those with baseline FVC % predicted <50% (HR 9.77, 95% CI 4.01–23.8; p<0.001) (figure 1b). Sensitivity analysis with baseline FVC % predicated as a continuous variable showed that every 5-percentage-point decrement in FVC % predicted was associated with increased risk by 15% (HR 1.15, 95% CI 1.06–1.25).

*FIGURE 1: Study cohort and transplant-free survival by baseline forced vital capacity (FVC) % predicted. a) Flow diagram of the included population. b) Transplant-free survival by baseline FVC % predicted among patients with stable non-idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (non-IPF) interstitial lung disease (ILD). #: Cox proportional hazards model was fit to estimate hazard ratios, adjusting for age, sex, smoking history, ILD subtypes, usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, baseline diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide, immunosuppressant, and anti-fibrotic agent use. HR: hazard ratio; IPF: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; PFT: pulmonary function test.*

Subgroup analyses explored four potential effect modifiers: 1) FVC % predicted trajectory during a stable period (decline or no change (≤0%) versus improvement (>0%)); 2) ≥10% DLCO decline (yes/no); 3) immunosuppressive use (yes/no); and 4) antifibrotic use (yes/no). The association between FVC % predicted <80% and increased risk of lung transplantation or death was more pronounced in patients whose FVC remained unchanged or fell (≤0%) (adjusted HR 3.05, 95% CI 1.35–6.92); in those without a ≥10% DLCO decline (HR 2.68, 95% CI 1.42–5.06); among individuals with (HR 5.42, 95% CI 1.59–18.5) or without immunosuppressants (HR 3.43, 95% CI 1.35–8.70); and in those not treated with antifibrotics (HR 2.36, 95% CI 1.31–4.28); interaction p-values were not significant. Results were robust in sensitivity analyses redefining “stable ILD” using 3% and 7% FVC cut-offs and in a cause-specific Cox model for all-cause mortality, remaining consistent with the primary analysis.

Previous studies in both IPF and non-IPF ILDs have shown that a lower FVC predicts worse outcomes [7–9]; however, to our knowledge, our study is the first to demonstrate that poor clinical outcomes can occur even among patients who do not meet the established criteria for physiological progression based on FVC decline. Subgroup analyses further revealed that among patients with minimal FVC % predicted decline (between −5% and 0%) and those whose DLCO % predicted remained stable over one year, lower FVC % predicted was still associated with a worse prognosis.

Although a lower FVC % predicted inevitably indicates some prior loss of lung function, current progression definitions hinge on documented decline during follow-up, and therefore do not capture disease burden that has accrued before the first post-diagnosis PFT. Consequently, patients who arrive with markedly impaired FVC but exhibit no further decline may be labelled stable, even though substantial progression has already taken place. Notably, in subgroup analyses restricted to patients whose DLCO remained stable over the first year, a lower baseline FVC % predicted was still associated with an increased risk of death or lung transplantation. Our findings highlight an important limitation and identify a clinically important group that can be overlooked by progression-based frameworks. One plausible explanation for this blind spot is the reliance on a fixed absolute FVC threshold [10]: a 5-point decline represents a much larger proportional loss when the starting value is already low, so absolute cut-offs can underestimate progression in severely impaired patients [11]. Beyond progression status, careful attention to baseline FVC % predicted, together with the extent of ILD on computed tomography – which is prognostic and used to determine eligibility in antifibrotic trials [12, 13] – could identify these vulnerable patients earlier and guide more appropriate management.

This study has several limitations. Because it is observational, residual confounding may persist, particularly from unmeasured functional status or performance level. Generalisability is uncertain because participants came from two tertiary referral centres; additionally, ∼85% of the cohort was identified from patients who underwent an extended myositis serologic panel, likely increasing the proportion meeting IPAF criteria and limiting applicability to settings with different testing practices. Excluding patients without paired PFTs may have introduced selection bias, especially against those with higher baseline FVC. Misclassification from PFT variability is possible around the 5-point absolute FVC threshold; nonetheless, results were consistent when using 3% and 7% cut-offs. Finally, restricting progression to the lung function component alone can omit patients who deteriorate slowly or whose course is driven mainly by symptomatic or radiographic changes. Accordingly, adding a baseline FVC threshold to current PPF definitions should not be assumed to improve prognostic performance without external validation. Future studies should incorporate composite progression criteria that include radiographic findings and respiratory symptoms and test whether patients with low baseline FVC but no early decline, a group not represented in INBUILD [14, 15], derive antifibrotic benefit.

In conclusion, among non-IPF ILD patients whose FVC declined by less than 5% predicted over 1 year, a low baseline FVC was still associated with poorer transplant-free survival. This association persisted even in the absence of observed disease progression, indicating that lower baseline FVC may still serve as a useful marker to identify patients who warrant closer monitoring.
